newsitem.title: UKRAINE: UKRAINE, POLAND TO MAKE NEW START AFTER BLOODY PAST.
newsitem.headline: UKRAINE, POLAND TO MAKE NEW START AFTER BLOODY PAST.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski arrived in Ukraine on Tuesday to make a new start in relations between the two countries after centuries of conflict and distrust.

"This visit must end the saga of very difficult historical relations between Poland and Ukraine," Kwasniewski said after co-chairing a joint meeting of a special security and cooperation committee with President Leonid Kuchma.
"We want to broaden the possibilities for young Poles and Ukrainians, for our citizens, but we also want these relations to have an impact on the regional situation and the whole of Europe," he said.

Kwasniewski and Kuchma are due to sign a declaration of reconciliation on Wednesday, burying the horrors of mutual blood-letting between the neighbouring nations which began in the 17th century and ended after World War Two.

Kuchma announced that Kwasniewski had been chosen to become the third foreign politician after Azeri leader Haydar Aliyev and Georgia's Eduard Shevardnadze to receive Ukraine's highest award -- the Order of Yaroslav the Wise.
Ukrainian Cossacks fought Polish troops in the 17th and 18th centuries in wars that ended with Kiev concluding a treaty with Russia and losing its independence.
Western Ukrainians, under Polish rule between the two world wars, were under pressure from Warsaw to stay within Poland and abandon creation of an independent state.

But the most painful memories which overshadow Ukrainian-Polish relations concern the killings of 34,650 Poles by the Ukrainian Insurrectionary Army (UPA) in the western Ukrainian region of Wolyn after 1943.
Poland deported more than 150,000 Ukrainians from its southeastern regions to the north and west to crush the rebels in 1947 in what was called "Operation Wisla".
Open debates of these and other politically sensitive events have only become possible since the break-up of the former Soviet Union in 1991.
Relations have gradually improved since and Poland was the first country to recognise Ukrainian independence.
Both states consider each other strategic partners and Warsaw sees the presence of Ukraine as a buffer next to Russia as good for its security.
Unlike Russia, Ukraine supports Poland's bid to join the NATO defence alliance but has not applied for membership itself, though it is seeking security guarantees.
But Kwasniewski said Russia should not be excluded from the European security system.

"If we want to achieve security in Europe then NATO enlargement should not turn its back on Russia," he told reporters. "The Russian Federation is an important partner in building a system of mutual trust and efficient security in Europe." '
